subject: Business
scope: Introductory business models using hypothetical data, not investment advice or a complete board specification.
objectives: Distinguish fixed, variable and total costs.
Evaluate the limitations of a break-even model.

notes.heading: Classifying costs within a stated range
paragraphs: A fixed cost does not change with output over the period and relevant range being considered. Rent might remain fixed during a lease even if production falls, but expanding into another building can increase it. A variable cost changes with output; in a simple linear model, each additional unit uses the same amount of material at the same price. Total variable cost equals variable cost per unit multiplied by output. Total cost adds fixed cost to total variable cost. Classification depends on context: labour may be salaried, paid per unit or include both elements. Always state the period and distinguish total amounts from amounts per unit.

notes.heading: Contribution and break-even
paragraphs: Revenue equals selling price per unit multiplied by units sold. Contribution per unit is selling price minus variable cost per unit. Each sale contributes this amount toward fixed costs; once fixed costs are covered, additional contribution increases operating profit in the model. Break-even occurs where total revenue equals total cost. If contribution per unit is positive, break-even quantity equals fixed costs divided by contribution per unit. For indivisible products, round a non-integer result upward when finding the smallest whole number of units needed to avoid a loss. If contribution is zero or negative while fixed costs are positive, increasing output cannot produce break-even under these assumptions.

notes.heading: Using a model without mistaking it for a forecast
paragraphs: The margin of safety is actual or forecast sales minus break-even sales, expressed in units or as a percentage of the stated sales figure. It describes how far sales could fall before the model predicts a loss. A larger margin does not guarantee survival: customers may pay late, costs may change and the business may lack cash despite recording profit. Break-even analysis usually assumes constant prices and unit variable costs, fixed costs within a relevant range, and that produced units are sold. Discounts, capacity constraints and a changing product mix can invalidate those assumptions. A sound recommendation combines the calculation with evidence about demand, capacity, quality and cash flow, rather than treating the break-even number as a sales forecast.

notes.heading: Sensitivity and decisions under limited capacity
paragraphs: A break-even calculation is most useful when paired with sensitivity analysis: change one assumption and examine how the result changes. If fixed costs rise, the contribution needed to cover them rises. If selling price falls while variable cost stays unchanged, contribution per unit shrinks and more sales are required. These conclusions rely on contribution remaining positive and the business being able to make and sell the additional units.

Capacity can make a mathematically calculated break-even level operationally unreachable. A workshop capable of producing 80 units cannot cover a modelled 100-unit threshold without changing capacity, price, cost or product mix. A proposed expansion may itself increase fixed costs, so the threshold must be recalculated rather than assumed constant. For a decision, distinguish relevant future changes from costs already incurred, while following the question's stated model. Qualitative factors such as reliability, staff workload and customer response also matter. Finish a recommendation by identifying which assumption would most change the conclusion and what evidence would help test it.

notes.heading: Capacity can rule out a calculated break-even point
paragraphs: A break-even calculation identifies a sales quantity under a stated cost and price model. It does not establish that a firm can produce or sell that quantity. Compare the result with capacity, expected demand and the relevant time period. If capacity is below break-even, calculate the loss at capacity before suggesting a change. Increasing price, lowering variable cost and reducing fixed cost affect different parts of the model; none is guaranteed to be feasible. Distinguish unit contribution from total profit: contribution first covers fixed costs. The fictional figures here teach model interpretation and are not a recommendation for a real investment or business decision.

workedExamples.prompt: A workshop has fixed costs of 600 currency units, a selling price of 15 and variable cost of 9 per item. Find break-even output.
steps: At 100 sales, revenue is 1500 and total cost is 600 + 900 = 1500.

workedExamples.prompt: For the same workshop, calculate modelled profit and margin of safety at 140 sales.
steps: Margin of safety is 140 − 100 = 40 items, or 40 ÷ 140 × 100 ≈ 28.6% of sales.
workedExamples.answer: Profit 240; margin of safety 40 items, approximately 28.6%.

workedExamples.prompt: A product has fixed costs of 500 and contribution of 5 per unit, but maximum period capacity is 80 units. Evaluate break-even feasibility.
steps: Capacity is below the required output.
At full capacity, contribution is 400 and modelled profit is -100.
workedExamples.answer: Break-even is infeasible within current capacity under these assumptions.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional workshop has monthly fixed costs of 1,200 units, price 18 per item and variable cost 10 per item. Capacity is 120 items per month. Find break-even output and profit at capacity.
workedExamples.answer: Break-even output is 150 items; at capacity the workshop makes a loss of 240 units.

misconceptions.correction: They are fixed only within the stated time period and relevant range.

misconceptions.claim: Break-even output predicts how many customers will buy.
misconceptions.correction: It identifies a cost-revenue threshold, not demand.

flashcards.front: What makes a cost fixed in a break-even model?
flashcards.back: It does not change with output within the stated period and relevant range.

flashcards.front: How is contribution per unit calculated?
flashcards.back: Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit.

flashcards.front: When does fixed cost divided by contribution give a meaningful break-even quantity?
flashcards.back: When contribution per unit is positive and the linear model assumptions apply.

flashcards.front: How is margin of safety in units calculated?
flashcards.back: Actual or forecast sales units minus break-even sales units.

flashcards.front: Why can a profitable business still have a cash shortage?
flashcards.back: Cash receipts and payments may occur at different times from the recognition of revenue and expenses.

flashcards.front: What does sensitivity analysis add to a break-even figure?
flashcards.back: It shows how the conclusion depends on assumptions such as price, unit variable cost and fixed cost.

flashcards.front: Why compare break-even output with capacity?
flashcards.back: A calculated sales threshold may be physically unattainable in the stated period.

flashcards.front: How does contribution differ from profit?
flashcards.back: Total contribution is sales revenue less variable costs; profit also subtracts fixed costs.

questions.prompt: Which measure equals selling price minus variable cost per unit?
solution: Separate unit amounts from total amounts.
The difference contributes toward fixed costs and then profit.

questions.prompt: Fixed costs are 900, price is 20 and variable cost is 14 per unit. Find break-even output in units.
A product contributes 8 per unit and fixed costs are 1000. Calculate modelled operating profit at 180 sales.
A manager lowers price and claims break-even sales must become easier to achieve. Evaluate this claim assuming unit variable cost stays unchanged.
questions.answer: Lower price reduces contribution per unit and raises break-even units if contribution remains positive. Demand might increase, but that needs evidence and sufficient capacity. A lower price alone does not guarantee that the higher threshold will be reached.
solution: Relate that change to the break-even denominator.
Distinguish the threshold from uncertain customer demand.
markingPoints: Explain higher break-even units under the stated conditions.
Give a qualified demand or capacity judgement.

questions.prompt: Why can investing in more capacity fail to improve a business's margin of safety even if it permits more production?
questions.answer: Investment may increase fixed costs and therefore break-even output, while demand may not rise enough to sell the additional capacity. Production capacity is not the same as realised sales.
solution: Identify a possible increase in fixed costs.
Relate it to the break-even threshold.
Distinguish capacity from uncertain customer demand and actual sales.
markingPoints: Identify a possible increase in fixed costs.
Relate it to the break-even threshold.
Distinguish capacity from uncertain customer demand and actual sales.

questions.prompt: A fictional workshop has monthly fixed costs of 1,200 units, price 18 per item and variable cost 10 per item. Capacity is 120 items per month. Find break-even output and profit at capacity.
questions.answer: Break-even output is 150 items; at capacity the workshop makes a loss of 240 units.

questions.prompt: A learner calls the 960 units of contribution at capacity a profit. Explain the omission and calculate the price needed to break even at 120 sales if all other assumptions stay fixed.
questions.answer: Fixed costs were omitted. Required price is 20 units per item, assuming 120 sales still occur.
solution: Contribution 960 must cover fixed costs 1,200 before any profit exists.
Adding variable cost 10 gives price 20, but unchanged demand at that price is an assumption.
markingPoints: Contribution 960 must cover fixed costs 1,200 before any profit exists.
Adding variable cost 10 gives price 20, but unchanged demand at that price is an assumption.

revisionChecklist: Label every amount as total or per unit.
Check contribution is positive before dividing.
State assumptions and distinguish profit from cash.
Explain the reasoning in “Check commercial feasibility” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.
